paragraphs.text: A threnodia, a doleful ditty. In all ages things joyful and sorrowful were made up in songs and ballads for popular use.
paragraphs.anchor: Moreover take thou up a lamentation.

paragraphs.text: Those four last kings - princes rather than kings, because vassals to Egypt and Babylon - who, by starting unnecessary wars, wrought their own and their country’s ruin.
paragraphs.anchor: For the princes of Israel.

paragraphs.text: Whereby is meant thy city of Jerusalem and people of the Jews, who took these four for their kings, and soon had enough of them.
paragraphs.anchor: What is thy mother?

paragraphs.text: So called for her nobleness, courage, and cruelty.
paragraphs.anchor: A lioness.

paragraphs.text: Alludit ad coitum It signifieth that this state, by conversing with other heathen princes, had been corrupted by them and conformed unto them.
paragraphs.anchor: She lay down among lions.

paragraphs.text: From whom they took in but few good principles for young princes. Wickedness is soon learned Of a certain prince of Germany it was said, Esset alius si esset apud alios, his company undid him: So it did Julian the apostate.
paragraphs.anchor: She nourished her whelps among young lions.

paragraphs.text: This was Jehoahaz.
paragraphs.anchor: And she brought up one of her whelps.

paragraphs.text: Cunning and cruel, and having never a good property, though the son of good Josiah; who might better have said than that pope did of his wicked son, Caesar Borgia, Haec vitia me non commonstratore dedicit, He never learned it of his father.
paragraphs.anchor: It became a young llon.

paragraphs.text: He was a very cannibal to his subjects, and made no more conscience to undo a poor man, to seek and suck his blood, than to eat a meal’s meat when hungry. {Psa 14:4}
paragraphs.anchor: It devoured men.

paragraphs.text: His lion-like disposition and practices were soon noised and noticed.
paragraphs.anchor: The nations also heard of him.

paragraphs.text: As lions are taken by their hunters. Tyrants hold not their own long those beasts are "made to be taken and destroyed"; as Nero, whom the senate judged to death as an enemy to mankind; {a} and as Commodus, who was, saith Orosius, cunctis incommodus, a mischief to mankind.
paragraphs.anchor: He was taken in their pit.

paragraphs.text: {a} Ex condicto omnes conveniunt ut eum capiant.
She looked for Jehoahaz’s return out of Egypt, as Sisera’s mother did for his safe and victorious return from the battle; but all in vain. "The hope of the hypocrite shall perish."
paragraphs.anchor: Now when she saw that she had waited and her hope was lost.

paragraphs.text: A brat of the same breed, and of no better condition. Judea changed her lords oft, but not her miseries. So did Rome in the times between Augustus and Constantine the Great; the names of those few of them that were good might be written within the compass of a signet, as one said. Scarce any of them died a natural death, unless it were Vespasian, qui solus imperatorum mutatus in melius, {a} who also was the only emperor that became better by his preferment.
paragraphs.anchor: Then she took another of her whelps.

paragraphs.text: {a} Tacitus.
Of whom he learned to king it, and to lionise it. See Eze 19:2-3.
paragraphs.anchor: He went up and down, &c.

paragraphs.text: To pull his subjects, and to make havoc, as our Henry III did, who was therefore called Regni dilapidator. destroyer of the kingdom.
paragraphs.anchor: Learned to catch the prey.

paragraphs.text: As Eze 19:3; see Jer 20:17.
paragraphs.anchor: And devoured men.

paragraphs.text: He had made them desolate, and bereft them of their right owners, whom he had devoured, and then seized them for himself. Some read and render it, He knew their desolate widows - i.e., He first killed up their husbands, and then lay with the widows: the men he devoured, the women he deflowered. Such work this wicked prince made, till God took him in hand; as he did also the other three here lamented, of whom may be said, as Plutarch doth of Galba, Otho, and Vitellius, emperors, that they were like kings in a tragedy, which last no longer than the time that they are represented on the stage.
paragraphs.anchor: And he knew their desolate places.

paragraphs.text: Nebuchadnezzar, with the neighbour nations his auxiliaries.
paragraphs.anchor: Then the nations set against him on every side.

paragraphs.text: As they did also over the two last kings, though not here specified, Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, because they chose rather to run the hazard of ruin by rebellion, than to continue safely with slavery.
paragraphs.anchor: They spread their net over him.

paragraphs.text: See Eze 19:4, an ordinary way of taking lions, as Pliny telleth us. Leones maxime foveis capiuntur.
paragraphs.anchor: He was taken in their pit.

paragraphs.text: Or, Hooks. As lions are not looked upon, but through a grate. In claustrum. God knows how to hamper the most truculent tyrants, as he did also Bajazet.
paragraphs.anchor: And they put him in ward in chains.

paragraphs.text: Into some strong tower, or rock, where he died; and his body was afterwards thrown out upon a dunghill. {Jer 22:18}
paragraphs.anchor: They brought him into holds.

paragraphs.text: The same lamentation is here continued, though under another parable - viz., of a wasted vine. Jerusalem was once a generous fruitful spreading vine. It began to be so again in some sort under Zedekiah, if he could have been contented. See on Eze 17:5; Eze 17:8.
paragraphs.anchor: Thy mother is like a vine in thy blood.

paragraphs.text: So firm were the branches of this vine, so many and likely to succeed him in the kingdom were Zedekiah’s children; his nobles also were men of great parts, and fit for greater employments.
paragraphs.anchor: And she had strong rods for sceptres.

paragraphs.text: High she grew, and in addition high minded, and so ripe for ruin.
paragraphs.anchor: And she appeared in her height.

paragraphs.text: And so thrown with a force to the ground, as a man doth a dry or barren plant.
paragraphs.anchor: But she was plucked up in fury.

paragraphs.text: See Eze 17:10. It is ventus urens et exsiccans; burning and drying wind this was Nebuchadnezzar and his army.
paragraphs.anchor: The east wind dried up her fruit.

paragraphs.text: Babylon was no wilderness, but fruitful beyond credulity, {a} But the poor captive Jews had little joy from it, for some time at least.
paragraphs.anchor: And now she is planted in a wilderness.

paragraphs.text: In terra sicca et sitioulosa. So it was to them, though never so well watered, because they wanted there the waters of the sanctuary, and many other comforts of their own country. See Psa 137:1-6
paragraphs.anchor: In a dry and thirsty ground.

paragraphs.text: {a} Herodot., lib. i. cap. 193; Plin., lib. vi. cap. 26.
i.e., Zedekiah, by his perjury and rebellion, hath ruined all, set all on a light fire.
paragraphs.anchor: And fire is gone out of a rod of her branches

paragraphs.text: None to speak of till Shiloh come. Rulers indeed they had after this and governors, {Hag 2:21} but no kings of their own nation.
paragraphs.anchor: So that she hath no strong rod, &c.

paragraphs.text: See on Eze 19:1.
paragraphs.anchor: This is a lamentation.

paragraphs.text: Jerusalem plangitur et plangetur. The nation of the Jews shall never want matter for mourning.
paragraphs.anchor: And shall be for a lamentation.
